Genomic and clinical landscape of RAS mutations in acute myeloid leukemia
abstract: RAS mutations are recurrent in acute myeloid leukemia (AML); yet, their genomic and clinical landscape remain poorly characterized. We analyzed centralized molecular profiling data in 8,553 patients with newly diagnosed AML. Of these, 1,775 (21%) harbored RAS mutations: NRAS in 1,103 (13%), KRAS in 445 (5%), and both in 227 (3%). RAS mutations primarily clustered in P-loop hotspots (G12/G13, 70%), with NRAS showing higher Q61 mutation prevalence (24% vs. 9%) and KRAS showing additional K117/A146 hotspots. Multiple RAS mutations occurred in 23% of patients. Convergent evolution of RAS signaling mutations emerged as a key feature of RASmut AML. RTK/RAS pathway mutations were non-uniformly enriched: PTPN11, KIT and FLT3-TKD mutations were positively associated, CBL mutations showed no association, and FLT3-ITD mutations were negatively associated. The prognostic impact of RAS mutations was dependent on the genomic background and treatment. In multivariate analyses in intensively treated patients, NRAS mutations showed opposing associations with overall survival (OS): adverse in patients with AML, myelodysplasia-related (HR=1.32, p=0.036) and favorable in those with NPM1 (HR=0.61, p=0.036) or FLT3-ITD (HR=0.63, p=0.048) mutations, among others. KRAS mutations predicted inferior OS (HR=1.41; p=0.003). In patients treated with non-intensive, venetoclax-based regimens, RAS mutations were associated with markedly inferior OS in patients with NPM1 (HR=2.98, p=0.007) or IDH1/2 mutations (HR=4.06, p<0.001). These data inform risk stratification and development of RAS-targeting strategies in AML.

title: Cases of High-Titer Inhibitor Formation After AAV Gene Therapy for Hemophilia A
abstract: Gene therapy for hemophilia A (HA) aims to provide durable hemostatic control and reduce treatment burden, but AAV-based products to date have limitations: inconsistent peak expression, declining factor levels, and immunogenicity causing transaminitis and expression loss. ASC618 (ASC Therapeutics, Milpitas, CA, USA) was developed as a second-generation gene therapy product to overcome some of these limitations, using ET3, a bioengineered chimeric human/porcine B-domain-deleted FVIII transgene, paired with a minimal liver promoter and liver codon optimization. In a phase 1/2 trial (NCT04676048), two patients received ASC618. Despite initial factor expression, both developed high-titer FVIII inhibitors and are now maintained on emicizumab prophylaxis. Although inhibitor titers have declined, both remain high-titer nearly two years after a single infusion. The best explanation for inhibitor formation is that the novel FVIII with the human-porcine hybrid construct (ET3) contained epitopes for which these patients had not developed tolerance despite both having more than 1000 exposure days to exogenous FVIII in the past. Although this trial has been halted, these cases provide important lessons for the development of future hemophilia gene therapies. They highlight the need for careful immunogenicity assessment when using bioengineered transgenes, even in previously treated patients with extensive factor VIII exposure.

title: A new reporter strategy reveals a subset of nonmigratory hematopoietic stem cells located in a dynamic bone marrow niche
abstract: Interactions of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) with the bone marrow microenvironment are critical to regulate stem cell function in homeostasis, emergency hematopoiesis and ageing. The dynamic behavior of endogenous HSCs in their niches has been challenging to study due to the complexity of markers required to define pure HSCs. Multiple recently developed reporter strategies advanced our capacity to identify HSCs in situ. Yet, they provide different levels of HSC enrichment and are frequently not stable in situations of perturbed hematopoiesis, leading to contradictory observations of HSC localization and migratory behavior. Here we employed a new double reporter strategy by combining the Hoxb5-mKO2 and Vwf-GFP reporters, that are stably expressed in homeostasis, stress and ageing. Hoxb5+Vwf+ cells represent a subset of highly pure and potent long-term HSCs with a platelet-biased pattern of differentiation, that are included in the populations identified by other reporter strategies. Intravital microscopy revealed Hoxb5+Vwf+ cells to be non-migratory in homeostasis, ageing, or following acute thrombocytopenia when these cells are actively proliferating, indicating that this non-migratory behavior is independent of cell cycle status. We found Hoxb5+Vwf+ HSCs in perivascular niches with a higher coverage by LepR+ mesenchymal cells but not preferentially located closer to megakaryocytes, when compared to Hoxb5+Vwf- cells. Nevertheless, stress-induced megakaryopoiesis following acute thrombocytopenia bring megakaryocytes into closer proximity of Hoxb5+Vwf+ HSCs, revealing previously unrecognized niche dynamics in HSC regulation during regeneration.

title: A randomized phase 2 study combining midostaurin, low-dose cytarabine and venetoclax in newly diagnosed AML ≥60 years
abstract: In randomized studies, addition of FLT3 inhibitors failed to improve survival in older patients with FLT3-ITD AML unfit for intensive chemotherapy. Although hypomethylating agents or low-dose cytarabine combined with venetoclax is standard, FLT3-ITD is an important mechanism of resistance and a barrier to improved survival. Recent studies show promise for the addition of gilteritinib or quizartinib to less intensive venetoclax-based therapy, however resulting marrow toxicity requires substantial reductions to administered treatment. The INTERVENE study (Investigating Novel Triplets to Extend Remission with VENetoclax in Elderly AML) (ACTRN12619001655134) examined the role of midostaurin (M) administered sequentially after low-dose cytarabine (L) combined with venetoclax (V) in patients with newly diagnosed AML ≥60 years with non-adverse karyotype. After a run-in phase (n=18) established that LDAC combined with venetoclax from days 1-28 and midostaurin from days 11-28 was tolerable, 120 patients were randomized 2:1 to receive either LVM or LV. For the primary endpoint, LVM did not improve composite complete remission (CRc), compared to LV (72% vs 68%). Combining midostaurin with LV enhanced CRc among the sub-group of patients (n=29) with FLT3-ITD (82% vs 57%, difference = 25%, 0.85 posterior probability true difference > 5%, 95% CrI: -10 to 59%) and improved FLT3-ITD clearance as measured by ultrasensitive NGS (65% vs 0%), resulting in longer OS (median 24.2 vs 8.8 months, HR=0.34, 95% CrI: 0.071 to 0.960), compared to LV. In conclusion, midostaurin combined with low-dose cytarabine and venetoclax is well-tolerated and may have a role in newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD AML unfit for intensive chemotherapy.

title: One CAR is good; are 2 CARs better?
No cure without consequence: HCT and CH in SCD
abstract: In this issue of Blood, Weeks et al 1 use targeted, deep-coverage, and error-corrected sequencing to define the genetic landscape of clonal hematopoiesis (CH) in adults with sickle cell disease (SCD) who underwent hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT).CH is an oligoclonal state driven by mutations in hematopoietic stem cells correlated with an increased risk for hematologic malignancy, several diseases of aging, and all-cause mortality.2 The extent to which CH is influenced by HCT has heretofore not been well characterized.The investigators assessed CH in both the transplant donors and recipients, thereby gaining crucial and novel insights into the mechanisms of CH emergence after HCT: donor-derived CH, persistent recipient CH, and newly emerged CH (see figure).Importantly, their findings suggest that CH sequelae in the posttransplant setting vary by the mechanism of clone emergence.

title: LIN28B: LINeage-dependent oncogene or tumor suppressor?
abstract: In this issue of Blood, using primarily human fetal cells and a CRISPR-Cas9induced chromosomal translocation model for infant leukemia, Ling et al 1 demonstrated that the fetal development-specific protein LIN28B is required for the initiation, maintenance, and B-cell identity of KMT2A:: AFF1 + infant B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL).In the ongoing debate over the role of LIN28B in infant leukemia, this study provides an important new puzzle piece that may be able to reconcile some of the previous, seemingly contradictory, findings.

title: Addressing CAR T-cell exhaustion through gene silencing
abstract: In this issue of Blood, Kim et al 1 report the results of a phase 2 trial of a new CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell product, anbalcabtagene autoleucel (anbal-cel), which has been engineered to be intrinsically resistant to exhaustion.In this trial of adults with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma, complete response (CR) rate was high at 67%, whereas rates of the key CAR T-cell toxicities, cytokine release syndrome and neurologic events, were modest at 57% and 14%, respectively.

Age-related anemia: a new microbial clue in old blood
Reframing APS thrombogenesis: a new PF4-driven mechanism
abstract: In this issue of Blood, Field et al 1 show that platelet factor 4 (PF4) forms a trimolecular antigenic complex with β2-glycoprotein I (β2GP1) and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), amplifying antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) autoantibody recognition and promoting thrombosis.

title: Chen L, Hu L, Liu X, et al. Single-cell profiling of ANKRD26 thrombocytopenia reveals progenitor expansion and polyploid apoptosis via JUNB-p21. Blood . 2026;147(17):1984-1998.
Peginterferon alfa-2a, bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide, and venetoclax in adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma
abstract: North American adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (NA-ATLL) has poor outcomes and limited therapeutic options. In a small case series, peginterferon-alfa-2a plus bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide, with selective venetoclax, suppressed HTLV-1, reduced circulating ATLL burden, supporting the prospective evaluation of this treatment modality.

title: Immunologic and Plasma-Dependent Mechanisms of Chronic Hemolysis and Hyperhemolysis in Sickle Cell Disease
abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is characterized by chronic hemolytic anemia and a propensity to acute exacerbations such as post-transfusion hyperhemolysis syndrome (HHS). While erythrocyte injury is secondary to hemoglobin S polymerization, the underlying pathophysiologic driver, the mechanism by which sickle erythrocytes are then removed from circulation is largely regulated by the immune system. Multiple pathways potentially play a role, driven by pathological changes within both the cellular and humoral immune system. The review examines what is known regarding changes to the outer membrane of the sickle erythrocyte (including the expression of phosphatidylserine (PS), mannose, CD47 and CD95/Fas), the role of plasma-derived opsonins (including Gas6, MFG-E8, Protein S, MBL, TSP1, IgG and C3b) and the macrophage receptors that recognize and bind these molecules (including TREM2, TIM4, MerTK, integrins αvβ3/5, CD206, CD209/DC-SIGN, SIRPα, FasL, FcR, and CR). Drawing upon the results of investigations by our group and others, we conclude with a proposed model for clearance of erythrocytes in SCD, in which chronic hemolysis predominantly occurs through extravascular erythrophagocytosis, whereas acute hemolytic events involve a shift towards intravascular hemolysis via complement assembly into the membrane attack complex, Fas-mediated erythronecroptosis, and heme-mediated ferroptosis. The process by which transfusion may accelerate these pathways and induce HHS is also considered.

title: CD8 T-cell exhaustion linked with CAR T-cell failure can be mitigated by a non-alpha IL2 receptor agonist
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CART19) therapy represents a breakthrough for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma (rrLBCL). However, suboptimal CART19 activity can lead to therapeutic failure and dismal outcomes. Through single cell RNA-sequencing of tumors at the time of progression from CART19, we show that a subset of tumor contain clonally expanded and proliferating populations of CART19 cells that acquire transcriptional features of dysfunction, suggestive of ongoing tumor cell engagement and chronic stimulation. Using an in vitro system to model this process, we show that iterative rechallenge of CART19 cells with target cells drives failure of tumor control associated with acquired transcriptomic features of T-cell dysfunction and reduced IL2 signaling. Pegenzileukin, a non-alpha IL2-receptor agonist, prevented CART19 dysfunction, improving T-cell expansion and tumor control in vitro. To test this concept in vivo, we developed a cell line model from a post-CART19 progression tumor that reproduces the response and failure kinetics observed in the originating patient. In vivo CART19 alone led to transient response followed by progression and secondary central nervous system relapse in this model, while the addition of pegenzileukin to CART19 led to the complete eradication of tumors. This provides mechanism-informed pre-clinical rationale for the use of non-alpha IL2 receptor agonists in combating T-cell exhaustion, a critical mechanism of CART19 failure.

title: Thrombin-mediated AutoRegulation of FVIII-mimetic antibodies enabling dynamic control of the hemostatic response
abstract: Emicizumab has transformed hemophilia A (HA) management by enabling effective subcutaneous prophylaxis independent of inhibitor status. However, its constitutive activity and lack of sensitivity to anticoagulant feedback contribute to excessive thrombin generation under certain conditions, particularly when combined with bypassing agents, a liability increasingly recognized as a class effect of FVIII-mimetic antibodies. We engineered an "AutoRegulated" (AR) FVIII-mimetic antibody by integrating a short thrombin cleavable peptide sensitive to the proteolytic activity of thrombin in the hinge region of both emicizumab arms. Insertion of the peptide did not impair structural integrity and biological function with AR-emicizumab demonstrating EC50 values of FVIII-mimetic activity and correction of blood loss in HA mice comparable to the parental emicizumab. However, the presence of thrombin-mediated AR enabled thrombin-responsive proteolytic inactivation upon exposure to supra-physiological thrombin levels, whereas the parental emicizumab remained unaffected. The dynamic control provided by AR efficiently reduced the procoagulant effects induced by co-administration of activated Prothrombin Complex Concentrates (aPCC). In thrombin generation assays, AR-emicizumab significantly attenuated the excessive thrombin peak observed with emicizumab. Similarly, in vivo, the presence of thrombin-mediated AR prevented platelet consumptive coagulopathy and reduced the microvascular pulmonary thrombosis induced by the parental molecule without affecting the systemic levels of the therapeutic antibody. This on-demand self-limiting mechanism aligns therapeutic activity with local hemostatic needs, may offer a promising therapeutic approach for HA patients, while establishing a generalizable strategy to improve the safety profile of next-generation hemostatic biologics.

title: Initial fixed low-versus moderate-dose hydroxyurea assignment in the long-term follow-up of the SPRINT cohort
abstract: In this pragmatic long-term follow-up of the SPRINT randomized trial cohort, rates of recurrent stroke and all-cause mortality did not differ significantly by an initial fixed low- versus moderate-dose of hydroxyurea over 4.9 years, with events clustering in the first year.

title: Molecular Underpinnings and Prevalence of Donor Cell-Derived Hematologic Neoplasms among Spanish Transplantation Centers
abstract: Donor cell-derived hematologic neoplasm (DDHN) is defined as a de novo hematologic malignancy originated from transplanted donor stem cells, distinct from the original recipient's disease (ORD). Its prevalence and biological mechanisms remain poorly defined. We conducted a nationwide study to estimate the prevalence of DDHN and characterize its clinical and molecular features. Twenty-four transplantation centers systematically reviewed their allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) cohorts. DDHN diagnosis required cytogenetic or molecular donor-origin confirmation. Molecular studies included germline-augmented targeted NGS, whole-exome sequencing, and donor-recipient comparative analyses. We identified 39 DDHN cases diagnosed between 2007 and 2025. Among 8,465 allo-HSCT performed between 2013-2022, DDHN prevalence was 0.28%, with a marked predominance after related-donor compared with unrelated transplantation (0.41% vs. 0.06%, p=0.0026). Median latency from transplantation to DDHN diagnosis was 56 months. Most DDHN were myeloid neoplasms, predominantly myelodysplastic neoplasms (51%) and acute myeloid leukemia (36%). Molecular characterization, available in 33 cases, revealed germline predisposition as the predominant underlying mechanism. Pathogenic/likely pathogenic germline variants were identified in 10 cases, involving DDX41 (n=7), CEBPA (n=2), and CHEK2 (n=1), all after a related-donor transplantation. DDX41-associated DDHN showed recurrent somatic hits and low genomic complexity. Donor-derived clonal hematopoiesis was confirmed in only one myeloid case involving U2AF1. These findings support inherited germline predisposition as the potential main molecular driver of DDHN after related allo-HSCT, reinforcing the recommendation for comprehensive germline evaluation of patients at ORD diagnosis prior to transplantation, followed by targeted cascade screening of candidate related donors.

title: Splicing Factor Mutations in Myeloid Malignancies
abstract: The discovery of recurrent somatic mutations affecting the RNA splicing machinery in 2011 revealed an unexpected class of driver mutations in hematologic malignancies. Remarkably, splicing factor (SF) mutations have emerged as some of the most frequent genetic lesions in myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and other dysplastic myeloid neoplasms, establishing aberrant RNA splicing as a major pathogenetic pathway in myeloid neoplasia. Subsequent studies have delineated their mutation-specific effects on RNA splicing and established their strong genotype-phenotype associations; consequently, SF mutations are now incorporated into contemporary disease classification and prognostic models. However, the mechanisms underlying their positive clonal selection and striking genotype-phenotype associations remain poorly understood, with co-mutations, clonal architecture, aging, and the hematopoietic microenvironment acting as important modifiers of disease expression. Elucidating how SF mutations interact with these modifiers to shape clonal fitness and disease phenotype remains a key challenge, while translating these biological insights into effective therapies represents the ultimate clinical goal.

title: Low Incidence of Cryptic Genetic Marrow Failure in Pediatric Severe Aplastic Anemia Following Negative Clinical Workup
abstract: Distinguishing inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFS) from acquired idiopathic severe aplastic anemia (SAA) impacts treatment decisions and long-term management. The diagnostic evaluation of SAA has evolved with advances in our understanding of IBMFS. The benefit of germline genetic testing to screen for IBMFS in the context of current comprehensive SAA evaluations has not been systematically assessed. Awaiting genetic testing can delay treatment for idiopathic SAA increasing the risk of life-threatening complications. This retrospective study investigates the incidence of cryptic IBMFS among pediatric patients with SAA evaluated with current standard-of-care clinical and laboratory assessments. Enhanced whole exome sequencing tailored to IBMFS genes was conducted for 153 patients with SAA. Comprehensive clinical and laboratory diagnostic data were available for 149 patients. No clinical or laboratory features of an IBMFS were identified in 113 patients (75.8%) and none harbored pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants diagnostic of IBMFS. At least one clinical finding suggestive of an IBMFS was identified in the remaining 36 patients (24.2%). Of these, one harbored a heterozygous pathogenic variant in SAMD9L and had a consistent clinical history. A second patient flagged by clinical evaluation had two pathogenic variants in ERCC6L2, although allelic phasing and therefore affected status could not be determined. For patients with a negative comprehensive workup for SAA utilizing current diagnostic clinical and laboratory evaluations, the risk of a cryptic IBMFS is low. For these patients, the low likelihood of benefit gained by awaiting genetic testing results must be weighed against the risks of treatment delay.

title: Multi-omics reveals evolution from CD7-negative T cell dysregulation to EBV-positive LPD after CD7 CAR-T therapy
abstract: EBV activation specifically occurs in a subset of patients following CD7 CAR-T therapy, subsequently leading to EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorder (EBV+ LPD), descriptively referred to as post-CD7 CAR-T lymphoproliferative disorder (PCLD) in this study. To comprehensively characterize PCLD, we employed single-nucleus RNA sequencing, ATAC sequencing, and Stereo-seq to perform multi-omic spatial profiling of PCLD, and compared it with classical post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD), EBV-negative diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (EBV- DLBCL) and normal lymph nodes. Infiltrating T cells in PCLD are uniquely characterized by CD7 negativity, exhibiting limited proliferation upon infection stimulation and impaired antiviral activity against EBV. Macrophages are recruited in an attempt to sustain viral clearance; however, the Macro_IDO1 subset emerges as the dominant macrophage population, exhibiting an immunosuppressive phenotype marked by elevated IDO1 expression. Spatially, macrophages, predominantly Macro_IDO1, aggregate to form an immunosuppressive niche that restricts T-cell infiltration and is enriched for inhibitory ligand-receptor interactions, including the PD-1/PD-L1 axis. T-cell function is further compromised, enabling sustained EBV infection of B cells and driving malignant transformation. EBV-driven B cells undergo plasmacytic differentiation and sustained proliferation, actively remodeling the microenvironment. This study provides a comprehensive molecular characterization of lymphoproliferative disorder following CD7 CAR-T therapy, elucidates spatial tumor-immune interactions, mechanisms of EBV-driven B-cell transformation and potential intervention strategies.

CD4+ T cells facilitate immunotherapy in ALK+ ALCL
abstract: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) is a malignant CD30 + aggressive, mature T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.T-cell cancers have highly diverse and often disappointing results when treated with immunotherapy.In this issue of Blood, Poggio et al 1 take up the challenge of identifying an ALCL-directed immunotherapy and show that CD4 + T cells play a key role in orchestrating the recruitment of natural killer (NK) cells and boosting cytotoxic T-cell activity.

title: Securing HMO coverage for HSCT
abstract: To address the concerns of targeting MYC in normal tissue homeostasis and to investigate on-target toxicities, Nishida et al performed elegant studies in humanized Crbn mice.Because murine Crbn is insensitive to many CELMoDs, 7 the authors used CrbnI391V mutant mice, which acquire the function of human CRBN-mediated protein.8 In these humanized Crbn mice, GT19630 was well tolerated, with no significant toxicities reported after 4 weeks of short-term treatment.However, effects of longer-term exposure to GT19630 will be important to assess, especially because MYC has a well-defined role in regulating the immune system, for which the authors present supporting RNA-sequencing data.This study highlights the importance of fundamental discoveries in underpinning transcription factor drug development, a type of target historically considered undruggable.This innovative and broad study describes the generation of a first-in-class small molecule that targets MYC through the generation of a hybrid PROTAC and molecular glue/CELMoD.The study includes a comprehensive mechanistic interrogation and demonstrates the broad efficacy of GT19630 across both solid and blood cancers.Traditionally, PROTACs have several limitations that have restricted their clinical application, including large molecular size, incompatible E3 ligase tissue expression, and poor membrane permeability, 9 but GT19630 seems to have overcome many of these obstacles.We await further data to ascertain the oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetics of GT19630 to further define its clinical applicability.Despite the absence of toxicities observed in CrbnI391V mutant mice, additional studies with prolonged treatment in larger animals, in which CELMoDs have activity more comparable to that in human, 10 are needed for progression to the clinic.This investigational MYC/GSPT1 degrader has demonstrated broad potential across multiple cancer types, supporting further clinical evaluation in diverse MYC-driven malignancies, which is an area of significant unmet clinical need.

Identifying novel genomic alterations in relapsed childhood B-ALL: a report from the Children's Oncology Group
abstract: Relapsed B-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) generally occurs due to the emergence of subclones resistant to therapy, leading to poor outcome. Here, we describe novel genomic alterations responsible for therapeutic resistance at a subtype level in a clinical trial (AALL1331) which randomized patients to blinatumomab and chemotherapy versus chemotherapy alone. We performed whole-genome and transcriptome sequencing on 288 patients (183 diagnosis/first relapse/germline trios and 105 additional patients with first-relapse samples) and analyzed 41 second-relapse samples. For ETV6::RUNX1, we showed that cases with gain of the fusion allele or with fusion transcript involving exon 5 of ETV6 and exon 4 of RUNX1 (E5-E4) had a higher risk of first relapse than cases with E5-E3. For the hyperdiploid subtype, we demonstrated that low modal chromosomal numbers (51-52) were more prone to first relapse than those with ≥53 chromosomes, with an additive effect of CREBBP mutations. We showed enrichment of IKZF1 alterations in the Philadelphia-like subtype and that NSD2 E1099K was commonly associated with relapse in TCF3::PBX1. Together, these new features accounted for 30% (n=55) of first relapses. Intriguingly, ~3% of relapses are related to secondary B-ALL or germline predisposition. We also compared genomic alterations at diagnosis and first relapse in relation to second relapse status in randomized patients, with TCF3::PBX1/NT5C2 linked to worse outcomes regardless of randomized arm. Together, our findings provide novel insights into the genomics of relapsed childhood B-ALL as well as in the context of blinatumomab therapy. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as # NCT0201853.
